column1: # title: ENG-205 Beowulf Part 3 — 4 Main Ideas

column2: The Geats loaded Hrothgar's treasure, horses, and war-gear onto their ship and sailed swiftly home to Hygelac's hall.

column1: Why the poet contrasts Hygd and Modthryth
column2: The poet contrasts generous Queen Hygd with cruel Queen Modthryth to show that a queen should weave peace rather than cause deaths.
Hygelac greeted Beowulf, admitted he had feared the voyage, and thanked God for his safe return.
Beowulf retold the fights with Grendel and his mother, adding new details such as Handscio's death and Grendel's dragon-skin pouch.
Beowulf reveals that Grendel carried a pouch made of dragon skins in which he meant to stuff his victims.

column1: The prediction about Freawaru and Ingeld
column2: Beowulf predicts that Freawaru's marriage will not end the Danish-Heathobard feud, because the sight of looted swords will stir up revenge.

column1: Why Beowulf gives his treasure to Hygelac
column2: Beowulf hands his Danish treasures to Hygelac because a loyal thane owes his rewards to his lord.
Hygelac gave Beowulf Hrethel's jeweled sword and a large estate with a hall and a throne.
The poet praises Beowulf because he never plotted against kinsmen or killed comrades in drink, unlike the treacherous men of other stories.
After Hygelac died in Friesland and his son Heardred was killed by the Swedes, the Geat kingdom passed to Beowulf.

column1: Why Beowulf first refuses the throne
column2: After Hygelac's death Beowulf refused Hygd's offer of the throne and instead supported young Heardred, out of loyalty to Hygelac's line.
A fugitive slave stole a jeweled cup from the dragon's hoard, and the enraged dragon began burning the Geats' land.
The last survivor buried his people's treasure and lamented that war had killed everyone who could use it, a picture of how every hall ends.
The dragon burned Beowulf's own hall, and Beowulf feared he had somehow broken God's law.

column1: Why Beowulf orders an iron shield
column2: Beowulf ordered a shield made entirely of iron because a wooden linden shield would burn in the dragon's fire.

column1: Why Beowulf fights the dragon almost alone
column2: Beowulf's pride and past victories made him scorn leading an army, so he chose to face the dragon by himself.
Before the fight, Beowulf recalls his fostering by Hrethel, Herebeald's accidental death, and the wars with the Swedes, sensing his own death.
Hrethel could not take revenge for Herebeald, because the killer was his own son, so he turned away from life.
Beowulf makes his final formal boast that he will win the gold or die, and tells his men the fight is his alone.

column1: The first clash with the dragon
column2: Beowulf's sword barely cut the dragon's scales and failed him, and the dragon engulfed him in fire.
Beowulf's hand-picked men fled into the woods, but Wiglaf remembered the gifts he had received and went to help.
Wiglaf reminded the others that they had pledged loyalty in the mead-hall in return for their armor, and said he would rather burn beside his lord.
Naegling snapped on the dragon's skull because Beowulf's strokes were too strong for any iron blade.
After the dragon bit Beowulf's neck, Wiglaf stabbed its belly to weaken the fire, and Beowulf finished it with his knife.
Beowulf asked to see the treasure, thanked God for winning it for his people, and ordered a barrow built at Hronesness.
Beowulf gave Wiglaf his gold collar, helmet, and mail shirt and called him the last of the Waegmundings.
Beowulf says he never started quarrels, never swore a false oath, and never murdered kinsmen, so God cannot blame him.
Wiglaf tells the deserters that they and their families will lose their lands, because death is better than a life of shame.
The messenger warns that once the Franks and the Swedes learn Beowulf is dead, old feuds will bring war on the Geats.
The poet says the hoard was cursed by those who buried it, which helps explain why winning it cost Beowulf his life.

column1: What happens to the dragon's hoard
column2: The Geats buried the treasure with Beowulf, leaving it "as useless to men now as it ever was."

column1: What happens to the dragon's body
column2: The Geats pushed the dragon's body over the cliff into the sea.
The Geats burned Beowulf on a pyre hung with helmets and shields, then built a barrow on the headland as his memorial.
Warriors rode around the barrow praising Beowulf as the kindest of kings and the keenest to win fame.
Beowulf's death leaves the Geats without a protector, so the poem ends by foreseeing their destruction by enemies.
The last survivor, the father's lament, and Beowulf's death all show that every hero, hall, and people must come to an end.
Wiglaf's courage and the others' desertion show that the heroic code depends on retainers repaying their lord's gifts in battle.
The dragon's gold, won at the price of Beowulf's life and then buried again, shows that treasure cannot save anyone from death.
The Swedish-Geat wars, the Heathobard feud, and Hrethel's unavengeable son show that feud shapes the fate of every people in the poem.
Beowulf says fate will decide the fight, while the narrator says only God may let someone open the hoard, which blends pagan and Christian ideas.
Beowulf's cremation and his burial with treasure in a barrow are pagan customs, even though the narrator speaks of God.
The poem contrasts young Beowulf defeating Grendel with old Beowulf dying against the dragon, which shows the full arc of a heroic life.
